newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee eases as capital import demand emerges.
newsitem.headline: India rupee eases as capital import demand emerges.

text.p: The Indian rupee weakened further on Thursday, but for once not because of central bank intervention.
Unexpected dollar buying from a bank covering customers' capital import demand caught the market unawares, dealers said.
Spot rupee closed at 35.83/84 against the dollar after touching a high of 35.86/87 during the day, they said.

The dollar opened unchanged from Wednesday's close at 35.80/81, a level established only after aggressive dollar buying by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and a large purchase by the State Bank of India (SBI), India's leading bank.
The market was drifting until unexpected dollar demand emerged from the state-run Bank of Baroda, normally a dollar seller in the inter-bank market, dealers said.
"After yesterday's dollar's rally, quite a few banks were caught short," the chief dealer at a foreign bank said.
The Bank of Baroda began buying at 35.81 and pushed the dollar up to 35.86. The market, used to RBI battling the rupee's rise in recent months, was in a near-panic, dealers said.
The rupee began recovering as soon the demand petered out.
"It was a classic demand and supply play," said a dealer.
"Their demand was not large," said a dealer. "I would put it between $30-50 million," he said.

The demand stemmed mainly from capital imports incurred by the Oil and Natural Gas Corportion, he said. Some demand came from the state-run utility firm National Thermal Power Corporation, dealers said.
Most bank dealers said Thursday's demand had nothing to do with an impending domestic oil price hike, although there was speculation oil firms need dollars to pay for imports.

"This may happen, but there is no sign of it yet," a dealer said. But, Thursday's action did signal the possibility of increased dollar demand for capital imports in the second half of financial year 1997/98 (April-March), he said.
Forward dollar premiums opened up but eased as the dollar's rally induced fresh exporter dollar sales, dealers said.
The six month annualised forward premium closed at 4.30 percent against the previous close of 4.42 percent.
